claim: Varying glucose over the range of concentrations that occur physiologically between the fed and fuel-deprived states (8 to 4 mM) has no significant effect on glucagon secretion in the perfused mouse pancreas.
source: Varying glucose over the range of concentrations that occur physiologically between the fed and fuel-deprived states (8 to 4 mM) has no significant effect on glucagon secretion in the perfused mouse pancreas or in isolated mouse islets (in vitro), and yet associates with dramatic increases in plasma glucagon.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from perfused pancreas experiments shown in Figure 1f

claim: Varying glucose over the range of concentrations that occur physiologically between the fed and fuel-deprived states (8 to 4 mM) has no significant effect on glucagon secretion in isolated mouse islets in vitro.
source: Varying glucose over the range of concentrations that occur physiologically between the fed and fuel-deprived states (8 to 4 mM) has no significant effect on glucagon secretion in the perfused mouse pancreas or in isolated mouse islets (in vitro), and yet associates with dramatic increases in plasma glucagon.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from isolated islet experiments shown in Figure 1g

claim: Varying glucose over the range of 8 to 4 mM associates with dramatic increases in plasma glucagon in vivo.
source: Varying glucose over the range of concentrations that occur physiologically between the fed and fuel-deprived states (8 to 4 mM) has no significant effect on glucagon secretion in the perfused mouse pancreas or in isolated mouse islets (in vitro), and yet associates with dramatic increases in plasma glucagon.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from insulin tolerance tests shown in Figure 1d,e

claim: Alpha-cells express high levels of the vasopressin 1b receptor (V1bR) gene (Avpr1b).
source: Alpha-cells express high levels of the vasopressin 1b receptor (V1bR) gene (Avpr1b).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from FACS-sorted alpha-cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c

claim: Activation of AVP neurons in vivo increased circulating copeptin.
source: Activation of AVP neurons in vivo increased circulating copeptin (the C-terminal segment of the AVP precursor peptide) and increased blood glucose; effects blocked by pharmacological antagonism of either the glucagon receptor or V1bR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 1c

claim: Activation of AVP neurons in vivo increased blood glucose.
source: Activation of AVP neurons in vivo increased circulating copeptin (the C-terminal segment of the AVP precursor peptide) and increased blood glucose; effects blocked by pharmacological antagonism of either the glucagon receptor or V1bR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from chemogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 1b

claim: The hyperglycemic effect of AVP neuron activation is blocked by pharmacological antagonism of the glucagon receptor.
source: Activation of AVP neurons in vivo increased circulating copeptin (the C-terminal segment of the AVP precursor peptide) and increased blood glucose; effects blocked by pharmacological antagonism of either the glucagon receptor or V1bR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing LY2409021 (glucagon receptor antagonist) blocked the hyperglycemic response in Figure 1b

claim: The hyperglycemic effect of AVP neuron activation is blocked by pharmacological antagonism of V1bR.
source: Activation of AVP neurons in vivo increased circulating copeptin (the C-terminal segment of the AVP precursor peptide) and increased blood glucose; effects blocked by pharmacological antagonism of either the glucagon receptor or V1bR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing SSR149415 (V1bR antagonist) blocked the hyperglycemic response in Figure 1b

claim: AVP mediates the stimulatory effects of hypoglycemia produced by exogenous insulin on glucagon secretion.
source: AVP also mediates the stimulatory effects of hypoglycemia produced by exogenous insulin and 2-deoxy-D-glucose on glucagon secretion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing V1bR antagonism and Avpr1b knockout reduced insulin-induced glucagon secretion in Figure 4a-d

claim: AVP mediates the stimulatory effects of hypoglycemia produced by 2-deoxy-D-glucose on glucagon secretion.
source: AVP also mediates the stimulatory effects of hypoglycemia produced by exogenous insulin and 2-deoxy-D-glucose on glucagon secretion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing V1bR antagonism reduced 2DG-induced glucagon secretion in Figure 4g

claim: The A1/C1 neurons of the medulla oblongata drive AVP neuron activation in response to insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
source: We show that the A1/C1 neurons of the medulla oblongata drive AVP neuron activation in response to insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing A1/C1 neuron inhibition reduced AVP neuron activity during insulin-induced hypoglycemia in Figure 5i-k

claim: AVP injection increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ in alpha-cells implanted into the anterior chamber of the eye.
source: AVP injection increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ in alpha-cells (implanted into the anterior chamber of the eye) and glucagon release.

claim: AVP injection increased glucagon release from islets implanted into the anterior chamber of the eye.
source: AVP injection increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ in alpha-cells (implanted into the anterior chamber of the eye) and glucagon release.

claim: Hypoglycemia increases circulating levels of AVP/copeptin in humans.

claim: AVP stimulates glucagon secretion from human islets.

claim: In patients with T1D, hypoglycemia failed to increase copeptin.

claim: In patients with T1D, hypoglycemia failed to increase glucagon.

claim: AVP is a physiological systemic regulator of glucagon secretion.

claim: The AVP-mediated mechanism of glucagon secretion becomes impaired in T1D.
source: These findings suggest that AVP is a physiological systemic regulator of glucagon secretion and that this mechanism becomes impaired in T1D.

claim: Glucagon is secreted from alpha-cells of the pancreatic islets.
source: Glucagon is secreted from alpha-cells of the pancreatic islets and has many physiological actions; most notably the potent stimulation of hepatic glucose production to restore euglycemia when blood glucose has fallen below the normal range (a process referred to as counter-regulation).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about glucagon physiology

claim: Glucagon potently stimulates hepatic glucose production to restore euglycemia when blood glucose has fallen below the normal range.
source: Glucagon is secreted from alpha-cells of the pancreatic islets and has many physiological actions; most notably the potent stimulation of hepatic glucose production to restore euglycemia when blood glucose has fallen below the normal range (a process referred to as counter-regulation).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about glucagon's role in counter-regulation, supported by citation to Frayn and Evans, 2019

claim: The importance of glucagon for glucose homeostasis is well established.
source: The importance of glucagon for glucose homeostasis is well established (Frayn and Evans, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frayn and Evans, 2019

claim: In both type-1 diabetes (T1D) and type-2 diabetes (T2D), hyperglycemia results from a combination of complete/partial loss of insulin secretion and over-secretion of glucagon.
source: In both type-1 diabetes (T1D) and type-2 diabetes (T2D), hyperglycemia results from a combination of complete/partial loss of insulin secretion and over-secretion of glucagon (Unger and Cherrington, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Unger and Cherrington, 2012

claim: Counter-regulatory glucagon secretion becomes impaired in both T1D and T2D.
source: In addition, counter-regulatory glucagon secretion becomes impaired in both forms of diabetes (particularly T1D), which may result in life-threatening hypoglycemia (UK Hypoglycaemia Study Group, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to UK Hypoglycaemia Study Group, 2007

claim: Impaired counter-regulatory glucagon secretion in diabetes may result in life-threatening hypoglycemia.
source: In addition, counter-regulatory glucagon secretion becomes impaired in both forms of diabetes (particularly T1D), which may result in life-threatening hypoglycemia (UK Hypoglycaemia Study Group, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to UK Hypoglycaemia Study Group, 2007

claim: There remains considerable uncertainty about the regulation of glucagon release and the relative importance of intra-islet effects and systemic factors.

evidence: Supported by citations to Gylfe, 2013 and Lai et al., 2018

claim: Hypoglycemia has been postulated to stimulate glucagon secretion via intrinsic mechanisms based on observations in isolated (ex vivo) islets.

claim: Hypoglycemia has been postulated to stimulate glucagon secretion via paracrine mechanisms based on observations in isolated (ex vivo) islets.
source: Based on observations in isolated (ex vivo) islets, hypoglycemia has been postulated to stimulate glucagon secretion via intrinsic (Yu et al., 2019; Rorsman et al., 2014; Basco et al., 2018) and/or paracrine mechanisms (Briant et al., 2018b; Vergari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Briant et al., 2018b; Vergari et al., 2019

claim: The islet is a critical component of the body's 'glucostat'.

evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2018

claim: The islet has the ability to intrinsically modulate glucagon output.
source: While it is indisputable that the islet is a critical component of the body's 'glucostat' (Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2018) and has the ability to intrinsically modulate glucagon output, it is clear that such an 'islet-centric' viewpoint is overly simplistic (Schwartz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2018 and general scientific knowledge

claim: An 'islet-centric' viewpoint of glucagon regulation is overly simplistic.

claim: Brain-directed interventions can profoundly alter islet alpha-cell function.

claim: Glucose-sensing neurons in the hypothalamus are key mediators of brain-directed modulation of alpha-cell function.

claim: Arginine-vasopressin (AVP) is a hormone synthesized in the hypothalamus.

claim: AVP neurons are divided into two classes: parvocellular AVP neurons and magnocellular AVP neurons.

claim: Parvocellular AVP neurons either project to the median eminence to stimulate ACTH and glucocorticoid release or project centrally to other brain regions.
source: AVP neurons are divided into two classes: parvocellular AVP neurons (which either project to the median eminence to stimulate ACTH and glucocorticoid release or project centrally to other brain regions) and magnocellular AVP neurons (which are the main contributors to circulating levels of AVP).

claim: The hyperglycemic response to 2DG was partially antagonized by pretreatment with the glucagon receptor antagonist LY2409021.

claim: Activation of C1 neurons (by targeted glucoprivation or chemogenetic manipulation) elevates blood glucose.

claim: Activation of C1 neurons elevates plasma glucagon.

claim: C1 cell lesions severely attenuate the release of AVP in response to hydralazine-evoked hypotension.

claim: The hindbrain VLM site may be a key regulator of AVP neuron activity during physiological stress.

claim: EPSCs evoked by opto-activation of A1/C1 neuron terminals were glutamatergic, as they were abolished by the AMPA and kainate receptor antagonist DNQX.

claim: c-Fos expression was increased in A1/C1 neurons following an insulin bolus.

claim: The deficiency of glucagon secretion in T1D may in part be explained by the major structural and functional changes that occur to islets in T1D.
